body:
This is an issue to track context on this problem.

We want to detect the supported CUDA version for hosts with an nvidia GPU for the torch backend feature, and additionally the compute capability (e.g. `sm80`) for wheel variants.

The classic way to do this is querying the CLI tool `nvidia-smi`. It's usually present, but there's no guarantee and no requirement for it to be present. It's wasteful and error prone to query a CLI tool, it runs against uv being a very fast tool, and against it being a highly reliable tool.

The generally correct way to get this information is to `dlopen()` the driver and ask it. We can't do this when uv is statically linked, e.g. when using the uv base image. There are ways to build probes or recruit the python interpreter for help, but both also seem slow and error prone. 

An easier way to get the driver version is to read (virtual) files, so right now we right `/sys/module/nvidia/version`, `/proc/driver/nvidia/version`, and `nvidia-smi`, in that order. That however doesn't work for the compute capability, and misses e.g. cuda-compat.

Codex came up with the plan below, which is complete but doesn't seem reasonable either. It's unclear how much of this we actually need to support: Which edge cases are actually relevant for torch users? Are there and simple and reliable APIs we can use to get this information?

---

### 1. Read the target environment

1. Read `NV_VARIANT_PROVIDER_FORCE_CUDA_DRIVER_VERSION`. If set, use it for the CUDA version and skip the driver-version probe.
2. Read `NV_VARIANT_PROVIDER_FORCE_SM_ARCH`. If set, use it for compute capability and skip the GPU probe.
3. Run the remaining steps in the target Python environment or container. For a cross-install, leave unspecified target values unknown.

### 2. Find the CUDA version on Linux with glibc

1. Open the target Python executable. Read its ELF class, machine, and `PT_INTERP` to identify the target architecture and loader.
2. For a normal `dlopen("libcuda.so.1")`, look for that **exact filename** in this order:
   1. The applicable `DT_RPATH` entries from the calling ELF objects, when the caller has no `DT_RUNPATH`.
   2. The target process’s startup `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, left to right.
   3. The caller’s `DT_RUNPATH`.
   4. Matching entries in `/etc/ld.so.cache`.
   5. The target loader’s default library directories.
   
   Expand `$ORIGIN` relative to the ELF object that defines it. Apply glibc’s architecture and hardware-capability rules. A wheel extension can be the caller. If its private search path or preload could change the winner and uv cannot determine which file wins, return `unknown`. [glibc lookup order](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/dlopen.3.html)
3. Follow the winning symlink with `std::fs::canonicalize`. Open that file with `std::fs::File::open`.
4. Read the ELF section `.note.cuda.fwd_compatibility`. Find the note owned by `NVIDIA Corporation` and parse its JSON field `"CUDA version"`. In the inspected `libcuda.so.570.124.06`, the literal value is **`"12.8"`**. [NVIDIA’s ELF parser](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/pull/1598)
5. If the note is absent, look up the exact binary build ID or its verified platform-specific driver release. The inspected Linux x86-64 `libcuda.so.550.67` reports **12.4**.
6. If the filename is generic, query the owner of the **resolved file** with `dpkg-query -S <path>` or `rpm -qf --qf '%{NAME}' <path>`. A verified `cuda-compat-12-8` owner gives **12.8**, including for Jetson’s `libcuda.so.1.1`. An unidentified file gives `unknown`.
7. Use that result directly. With both toolkits installed, putting `/usr/local/cuda-12.8/compat` first in `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` can change the winner from **550.67 → 12.4** to **570.124.06 → 12.8**. Removing that entry restores **12.4**. The kernel driver can stay at 550 throughout. [NVIDIA’s `cuda-compat` installation example](https://docs.nvidia.com/deploy/cuda-compatibility/forward-compatibility.html)

### 3. Find the CUDA version on native Windows x64

1. For the standard system-driver lookup, call `GetSystemDirectoryW()` and append `nvcuda.dll`. For a known application-private DLL selection, use that exact path. If the target architecture or selected path is unresolved, return `unknown`.
2. Call `GetFileVersionInfoSizeW(path)`, allocate the buffer, then call `GetFileVersionInfoW(path)`.
3. Call `VerQueryValueW` for `\VarFileInfo\Translation` to get the language and code page.
4. Call `VerQueryValueW` for `\StringFileInfo\<language><codepage>\ProductName`. Parse `NVIDIA CUDA <major>.<minor>[.<build>] driver`. An unrecognized value gives `unknown`. [Microsoft’s version-resource API](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winver/nf-winver-verqueryvaluew)
5. **Verified on driver 572.83.** Its INF installs `nvcuda_loader64.dll` as `System32\nvcuda.dll`. Both the loader and `nvcuda64.dll` contain `ProductName = NVIDIA CUDA 12.8.97 driver`. The implementation of `cuDriverGetVersion` writes `12080`, confirming **12.8** from the binary. This was package inspection, without a live Windows GPU. [NVIDIA driver package](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/drivers/details/242277/) · [Exact INF entry](/private/tmp/uv-nvidia-provenance.C5cQph80/win572.83/Display.Driver/nv_dispi.inf:12321)

### 4. Handle WSL’s projected driver

1. Run the Linux lookup first. If `/usr/lib/wsl/lib/libcuda.so.1` wins, it can be a loader shim. In 572.83, both the shim and the implementation lack the CUDA ELF note.
2. Use `libdxcore.so`’s `D3DKMTEnumAdapters3` or `D3DKMTEnumAdapters2`, then `D3DKMTQueryAdapterInfo` with the driver-store-path query. NVIDIA uses these calls to locate each active adapter’s driver directory. [NVIDIA’s WSL implementation](https://github.com/NVIDIA/libnvidia-container/blob/main/src/dxcore.c#L133-L201)
3. Open `<adapter driver directory>/libcuda.so.1.1`. Read `.note.gnu.build-id` and look it up in a verified WSL table. The inspected 572.83 implementation has build ID `f4499e13f26ff0f2a53ad6bef234cd1c84eb354e` and writes `12080` in `cuDriverGetVersion`. An unrecognized build or conflicting adapter results give `unknown`.

### 5. Find compute capability and match the wheel

1. **Linux PCI GPU.** Enumerate `/proc/driver/nvidia/gpus/*/information`. Read `Bus Location`, `GPU UUID`, and `Device Minor`. For each bus location, read `vendor`, `device`, `subsystem_vendor`, and `subsystem_device` under `/sys/bus/pci/devices/<bus-location>/`. [NVIDIA’s procfs implementation](https://github.com/NVIDIA/open-gpu-kernel-modules/blob/550.144.03/kernel-open/nvidia/nv-procfs.c#L139-L160) · [Linux PCI files](https://docs.kernel.org/PCI/sysfs-pci.html)
2. **Windows PCI GPU.** Call `CM_Get_Device_ID_List_SizeW` and `CM_Get_Device_ID_ListW` for present `PCI` devices. Call `CM_Locate_DevNodeW`, then `CM_Get_DevNode_PropertyW(DEVPKEY_Device_HardwareIds)`. Parse `VEN_`, `DEV_`, and `SUBSYS_`. [Microsoft’s PCI ID format](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/install/identifiers-for-pci-devices)
3. **Map the IDs.** For example, NVIDIA’s driver identifies `10de:2684` as an RTX 4090, and NVIDIA lists that GPU at **8.9**. Use subsystem IDs where needed. For integrated Jetson GPUs, read `/sys/firmware/devicetree/base/compatible` and use a verified SoC mapping. [NVIDIA driver ID table](https://github.com/NVIDIA/open-gpu-kernel-modules/blob/550.144.03/src/nvidia/generated/g_nv_name_released.h#L1007) · [NVIDIA compute capabilities](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda/gpus)
4. **Apply visibility.** Read `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` and `CUDA_DEVICE_ORDER`. In a Linux container, match device minors against exposed `/dev/nvidia<minor>` nodes. Use the highest visible compute capability. If an ordinal, MIG device, or WSL adapter cannot be mapped reliably, leave `sm_arch` unknown. [CUDA device enumeration](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/05-appendices/environment-variables.html)
5. **Select the wheel.** Match Python, ABI, and platform tags. Apply the wheel’s declared CUDA bounds to the selected driver’s API version. Apply `sm_arch` when declared. A known CUDA version with unknown SM can still select a CUDA-version-only wheel. The install-time probe never needs to call `cuInit`, `cuDriverGetVersion`, NVML, or `nvidia-smi`. [NVIDIA wheel property definitions](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/streamline-cuda-accelerated-python-install-and-packaging-workflows-with-wheel-variants/)
title: nvidia detection beyond `nvidia-smi`
